note: 20-question public sample from the private CNA batch 1 bank. Draft questions under expert review.

questions.stem: A resident in bed says she is short of breath. While waiting for the nurse, the nurse aide should help her into which position?
options: Supine, flat on her back with one pillow
Prone, lying on her stomach
Fowler's position, with the head of the bed raised
Side-lying on her left side with the head of the bed flat
questions.rationale: Raising the head of the bed (Fowler's or high Fowler's) lets the lungs expand more easily and helps breathing. Lying flat or face-down makes breathing harder.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: When helping a resident with moderate dementia get dressed, the nurse aide should
options: offer a choice among eight outfits.
explain all the steps at once before starting.
give one simple instruction at a time.
speak quickly so the task is done fast.
questions.rationale: People with dementia have trouble following several steps at once. Short, simple instructions, one at a time, with a limited choice of two outfits, help the resident take part in dressing.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: While making a resident's bed, the nurse aide finds a rosary under the pillow. The aide should
options: send it to the lost and found at the front desk.
throw it away with the soiled linens and the pillowcase.
give it to the roommate to hold until later.
handle it with care and put it back where she keeps it.
questions.rationale: Religious items are important personal belongings and are handled respectfully. The aide returns it to its place or asks the resident where she would like it.
questions.reference: 42 CFR 483.10, Resident rights (OBRA 1987 requirements for long-term care facilities).

questions.stem: When entering the room of a resident who is blind, the nurse aide should FIRST
options: move the furniture to make more space.
knock, say who they are, and explain why they are there.
speak loudly so the resident hears.
touch the resident's shoulder without speaking.
questions.rationale: Announcing yourself prevents startling the resident. Furniture and belongings are kept in the same places so the resident can find them. Vision loss does not affect hearing, so a normal voice is used.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: For a resident lying on her back, the nurse aide should check the skin MOST carefully over the
options: forehead and nose.
knees and front of the hips.
sacrum and heels.
palms of the hands.
questions.rationale: In the back-lying position, the most pressure falls on the back of the head, shoulder blades, elbows, sacrum, and heels. These bony areas need frequent checks and repositioning.
questions.reference: National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel. Pressure injury stages and prevention (2016, current).

questions.stem: The nurse aide sees smoke coming from a resident's room. Using RACE, what should the aide do FIRST?
options: Call the resident's family.
Rescue anyone in immediate danger.
Close all the windows in the building.
Use a fire extinguisher on the fire.
questions.rationale: RACE stands for Rescue, Alarm (activate the alarm and report), Contain (close doors and windows), and Extinguish or Evacuate. Removing people from immediate danger comes first.
questions.reference: Standard facility fire-response training (RACE and PASS); NFPA 101 Life Safety Code for health care occupancies.

questions.stem: A sign over a resident's bed says "NPO." This means the resident
options: needs to be fed by the aide.
may have unlimited fluids.
may have only clear liquids.
may have nothing by mouth.
questions.rationale: NPO means nothing by mouth: no food, no drinks, and usually no ice chips unless allowed. It is often ordered before surgery or tests. The aide removes the water pitcher and tells the resident why, as directed by the nurse.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: A resident tells the nurse aide, "I don't see the point in living anymore." The aide should
options: stay with the resident and tell the nurse right away.
promise to keep it a secret.
tell the resident not to talk like that.
change the subject to something cheerful so he stops thinking about it.
questions.rationale: A statement about not wanting to live is taken seriously every time. The aide listens, keeps the resident safe, and reports it to the nurse immediately. Promising secrecy or dismissing the statement delays help.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: When speaking with a resident who has hearing loss, the nurse aide should
options: shout close to the resident's ear so he can hear.
speak from behind the resident while giving care.
face the resident and speak clearly in a normal or lower tone.
speak quickly so the conversation does not tire him.
questions.rationale: Facing the resident lets him see facial expressions and lip movements. Speaking clearly in a lower pitch is easier to hear than shouting, which distorts sound. The aide also reduces background noise and checks that hearing aids are in and working.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: Standard precautions mean that the nurse aide should
options: treat all blood and body fluids as if they could be infectious.
use precautions only for residents with a known infection.
wear a gown and mask for every resident.
wash hands only after removing gloves.
questions.rationale: Standard precautions apply to every resident, every time, because many infections are not yet known. They include hand hygiene and using gloves and other protective equipment whenever contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin, or mucous membranes is expected.
questions.reference: CDC/HICPAC. Guideline for Isolation Precautions: Preventing Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings (2007, updated).

questions.stem: A resident drank one 8-ounce carton of milk. How many milliliters should the nurse aide record?
options: 240 mL
300 mL
80 mL
160 mL
questions.rationale: One fluid ounce is about 30 mL, so 8 ounces times 30 mL equals 240 mL. Intake is recorded in milliliters so that it can be compared with output.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: During passive range of motion exercises, the nurse aide should
options: have the resident move each joint without any help.
move each joint quickly past the point of resistance to stretch it fully.
skip any joints that the resident says feel stiff.
support the joint and move it gently, stopping if there is pain.
questions.rationale: In passive range of motion, the aide moves the joint for the resident, supporting the limb above and below the joint and moving slowly and gently. The aide never forces a joint past resistance and stops if there is pain, then reports it.
questions.reference: Credentia. NNAAP California Nurse Assistant Candidate Handbook, skills listing (Southern Region).

questions.stem: When walking a resident with a weak left leg using a transfer belt, the nurse aide should walk
options: slightly behind the resident on the right (strong) side.
slightly behind the resident on the left (weak) side.
in front of the resident, facing backward.
several steps behind the resident.
questions.rationale: Standing slightly behind on the weak side puts the aide where a fall is most likely and allows a firm hold on the belt with an underhand grasp. Walking in front blocks the resident's path, and several steps behind is too far to help.
questions.reference: Credentia. NNAAP California Nurse Assistant Candidate Handbook, skills listing (Southern Region).

questions.stem: A resident refuses his shower this morning. The nurse aide should
options: give him the shower anyway, since it is on the schedule and he needs to stay clean.
respect his choice, ask whether he would like it later, and tell the nurse.
skip the shower and not tell anyone.
tell him he will lose his privileges.
questions.rationale: Residents have the right to refuse care. The aide asks about the reason, offers another time or another option, and reports the refusal so the care team can follow up. Forcing care or threatening the resident violates his rights.
questions.reference: 42 CFR 483.10, Resident rights (OBRA 1987 requirements for long-term care facilities).

questions.stem: To measure a resident's urine output accurately, the nurse aide should read the graduate
options: while holding it up toward the light.
from above while it sits on the floor.
after adding water to reach a full mark.
on a flat surface at eye level.
questions.rationale: A graduated container is read on a flat surface at eye level so the line is not tilted or viewed from an angle. Nothing is added to the urine, and the container is not placed on the floor.
questions.reference: Credentia. NNAAP California Nurse Assistant Candidate Handbook, skills listing (Southern Region).

questions.stem: A resident asks the nurse aide to hand him his pills from the medicine cup the nurse left on the table. The aide should
options: put the pills in his drawer so he can take them later.
crush the pills into applesauce so he can swallow them.
tell the nurse, because giving medications is outside the aide's role.
hand him the pills and watch him swallow them, since the nurse already poured them.
questions.rationale: Nurse aides do not give medications, even ones a nurse has poured. A medicine cup left unattended is also a safety concern, so the aide notifies the nurse.
questions.reference: California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Div. 5, Ch. 2.5 (nurse assistant training and role); facility scope-of-practice policy.

questions.stem: Before feeding a resident who cannot feed herself, the nurse aide should position the resident
options: lying flat on her back.
sitting upright, as close to 90 degrees as possible.
with the head of the bed raised about 15 degrees.
on her left side with the head flat.
questions.rationale: Sitting upright lets food move down the esophagus and lowers the risk of choking and aspiration. Lying flat or nearly flat makes swallowing harder and raises the risk that food or fluid will enter the airway.
questions.reference: Credentia. NNAAP California Nurse Assistant Candidate Handbook, skills listing (Southern Region).

questions.stem: The normal resting pulse rate for an adult is
options: 20 to 40 beats per minute.
100 to 140 beats per minute.
60 to 100 beats per minute.
140 to 180 beats per minute.
questions.rationale: A resting adult pulse between 60 and 100 beats per minute is considered normal. A rate below 60 or above 100 is reported to the nurse.
questions.reference: Sorrentino SA, Remmert LN. Mosby's Textbook for Nursing Assistants. Elsevier (current edition).

questions.stem: Before giving perineal care, the nurse aide should provide privacy by
options: asking visitors to stay and watch so that they can learn.
closing the curtain and door and covering with a bath blanket.
leaving the door open so other staff can come help.
uncovering the resident completely to work faster.
questions.rationale: Privacy is a resident right and a beginning step of every skill. Closing curtains and doors and exposing only the area being cleaned protect dignity.
questions.reference: Credentia. NNAAP California Nurse Assistant Candidate Handbook, skills listing (Southern Region).

questions.stem: Before leaving a resident's room, the nurse aide should always
options: clip the call light to the curtain.
put the call light on the floor.
place the call light within the resident's reach.
turn off the call light so it does not ring.
questions.rationale: The call light is how a resident asks for help. Leaving it within reach is a safety step at the end of every task.
questions.reference: Credentia. NNAAP California Nurse Assistant Candidate Handbook, skills listing (Southern Region).
